title: No urine since morning
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; they are not targets. No doses are given. Your hospital’s protocol, the antibiogram and the attending nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on night duty in a provincial hospital in Iloilo. Mang Ernesto Bautista, 74, a retired fisherman with an enlarged prostate, was admitted this afternoon for weakness and poor intake. He stopped his prostate tablet a month ago when it ran out.

At 22:00 the intern, Dr. Joy Ramos, calls you. He has passed no urine for 10 hours. His creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL; it was 1.1 mg/dL at a check-up last year. He has lower abdominal discomfort, and his lower abdomen is dull to percussion. She asks: “Can I give him a diuretic?” This is acute kidney injury (AKI) until proven otherwise, and the question is where the urine is.

n1.prompt: What do you tell Dr. Ramos?

choices.text: Yes, give the diuretic and see whether the urine comes.
choices.feedback: A diuretic cannot push urine past an obstruction. A full bladder in an anuric man is a catheter, not a diuretic.
choices.then: An hour later there is still no urine and the discomfort is worse. You ask for a bladder scan: the bladder is distended. The nurse passes a urethral catheter, which drains 1,800 mL of cloudy urine.

choices.text: Run an intravenous fluid bolus first; he has been eating poorly and is probably dry.
choices.feedback: Poor intake can cause AKI, but a dull, tender lower abdomen and a man with prostate symptoms point to outlet obstruction. Fluid will not reach a bladder that cannot empty, and it can overload him.
choices.then: The nurse scans the bladder before the bolus finishes: it is distended. A urethral catheter drains 1,800 mL of cloudy urine.

choices.text: No diuretic. Scan or palpate the bladder now; if it is full, pass a urethral catheter, and call me back with the volume.
choices.feedback: In older men, bladder outlet obstruction from an enlarged prostate is the most common cause of obstructive AKI. Checking the bladder is the first step in every anuric patient, and the catheter is the treatment.
choices.then: The bladder scan shows a distended bladder. A urethral catheter drains 1,800 mL of cloudy urine.

n2.scene: Fifteen minutes later Dr. Ramos calls again. He has had a rigor. Temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 23, blood pressure 100/62 mm Hg. He is alert.

choices.text: This is sepsis with a urinary source until proven otherwise. Draw blood and urine cultures now, start an empiric antibiotic straight after, run fluids, and call the attending.
choices.feedback: His respiratory rate of 22 or more and systolic pressure of 100 or less give a quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score of 2, a flag for a poor outcome. Cultures before the first dose let you narrow therapy later; the antibiotic should not wait for them.

choices.text: Start the antibiotic at once and draw the cultures afterward when the lab comes.
choices.feedback: Speed is right, but cultures drawn after the first dose may grow nothing. With resistance common in Philippine hospitals, you will need that culture to narrow or change therapy.
choices.then: You ask the nurse to draw the cultures before the antibiotic is hung, and you call the attending.

choices.text: Send a urine culture and start the antibiotic when it grows something.
choices.feedback: A culture takes a day or more. A septic patient with qSOFA 2 needs an empiric antibiotic tonight, and blood cultures too.
choices.then: The nurse questions the plan. You draw blood cultures, plan the antibiotic, and call the attending.

choices.text: The fever is from the catheter passage. Give an antipyretic and review in the morning.
choices.feedback: Rigors, tachypnea and a falling pressure in a man with stagnant, cloudy urine are urosepsis. A night of waiting can become septic shock.
choices.then: At 00:30 his pressure is 94/58. You draw cultures, plan the antibiotic and call the attending.

n3.scene: His daughter shows you a photo on her phone: a urine culture from three months ago grew E. coli resistant to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. He took ciprofloxacin two months ago. The hospital antibiogram is on the ward wall.

choices.text: Oral ciprofloxacin, so he can go home sooner.
choices.feedback: His last isolate resisted it, and he took a fluoroquinolone in the past 12 months; the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) 2025 approach asks you to avoid both. A septic patient also needs intravenous therapy first.
choices.then: You pick an agent from the sepsis list that his old isolate was susceptible to, check the antibiogram, and review the dose with the pharmacist.

choices.text: The right agent from the sepsis list, at the full standard dose; his creatinine will improve now that he is drained.
choices.feedback: It may improve, but tonight his creatinine is 2.6. Doses come from the formulary, adjusted for kidney function with the pharmacist, and are reviewed as the creatinine changes.
choices.then: The pharmacist adjusts the dose for his creatinine clearance, with a plan to review it daily.

choices.text: From the IDSA sepsis list, an agent his old isolate was susceptible to, not a fluoroquinolone, with at least 80% susceptibility on the antibiogram; dose adjusted for his kidney function with the pharmacist.
choices.feedback: IDSA 2025 asks four questions in order: is there sepsis, what is the resistance risk, what are the patient factors, and what does the local antibiogram show. His own past culture is the strongest clue you have.

choices.text: Ceftriaxone, the ward’s usual choice; old cultures do not matter tonight.
choices.feedback: His previous E. coli resisted ceftriaxone. In sepsis, an antibiotic the organism is likely to resist leaves the infection untreated through the hours that matter most.
choices.then: The pharmacist flags the old culture. You change to an agent his isolate was susceptible to, with the dose adjusted for his kidney function.

n4.scene: His pressure is a little better. Since midnight he has passed 350 to 400 mL of urine every hour. The nurse asks what to do about it.
n4.prompt: What is your plan for the urine?

choices.text: Note it, and check his electrolytes with the morning bloods.
choices.feedback: Most post-obstructive diuresis is appropriate, but some patients keep losing water and salt and become volume depleted with abnormal sodium or potassium. A morning check can come too late.
choices.then: You change the plan: hourly output, electrolytes now and repeated, and a call to the attending to agree the replacement.

vitals.order: Hourly urine; electrolytes q4h; replacement per attending

choices.text: Hourly urine output, blood pressure and mental state; electrolytes now and repeated; agree the replacement plan with the attending.
choices.feedback: Retained urea, sodium and water leave first, and injured tubules may not hold salt or concentrate urine for a while. Measuring closely shows you where the diuresis is going; the attending sets the plan.

vitals.order: Hourly urine; electrolytes q4h; replacement per attending

choices.text: Replace every milliliter of urine with intravenous fluid, hour by hour.
choices.feedback: Matching replacement to output without thought keeps the diuresis going, because the kidney keeps excreting what you give.
choices.then: The attending, on the phone, asks for hourly measurement and electrolytes instead, with a replacement plan she will set.

vitals.order: Hourly urine; electrolytes q4h; replacement per attending

choices.text: Clamp the catheter for a few hours to slow the diuresis.
choices.feedback: Clamping re-creates the obstruction you just relieved, in a man with infected urine behind it.
choices.then: The nurse declines to clamp. You order hourly output and electrolytes, and call the attending for a replacement plan.

vitals.order: Hourly urine; electrolytes q4h; replacement per attending

n5.scene: At 06:00 his output is still 380 mL an hour, more than the plan expected. His pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Sodium is 149 and potassium 3.0 mmol/L. Rounds start at 08:00.

choices.text: Keep the plan running and present it at 08:00 rounds.
choices.feedback: Output above the plan with falling pressure and abnormal sodium and potassium is on the module’s stop-and-call list. Two hours is long enough to become much drier.
choices.then: The nurse insists. You call the attending with the numbers; she revises the replacement and asks for repeat electrolytes in two hours.

vitals.order: Replacement revised; repeat Na/K in 2 h

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus yourself and mention it to the attending at rounds.
choices.feedback: Treating the low pressure is reasonable, but the problem is the plan, and the sodium and potassium need new orders too. Replacement after relief of obstruction is set by the attending.
choices.then: The pressure rises a little. At rounds the attending revises the replacement and asks to be called next time.

vitals.order: Replacement revised; repeat Na/K in 2 h

choices.text: Call the attending now: urine output, blood pressure, heart rate, sodium and potassium, and what has been given since midnight. Ask for a revised replacement plan and read it back.
choices.feedback: This is exactly when to stop and call, per unit protocol, but always asking the attending nephrologist for guidance. Concrete numbers let her change the plan over the phone.

vitals.order: Replacement revised; repeat Na/K in 2 h

end.title: Day 4
end.text: The diuresis settles by day 2. The cultures grow E. coli, and the antibiotic is narrowed to the result, then switched to an oral agent once he improves. Ultrasound shows mild hydronephrosis on both sides that is resolving. His creatinine falls to 1.4 mg/dL. Urology plans the definitive treatment of his prostate; the antibiotic duration is individualized, because the duration trials excluded patients with obstruction and men with possible prostatitis may need longer.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • In every anuric patient, check the bladder first. A full bladder is a catheter, not a diuretic.
  • Fever after relief of obstruction is urosepsis until proven otherwise: cultures first, then the antibiotic without delay, and the attending told.
  • Choose the antibiotic by the IDSA 2025 steps: severity, the patient’s own past cultures and recent fluoroquinolone use, kidney function, and the local antibiogram.
  • After relief, measure the urine every hour. Replacing it milliliter for milliliter keeps the diuresis going; clamping re-obstructs.
  • Output above the plan with falling pressure or abnormal sodium or potassium means calling the attending now, with the numbers.

See Obstruction and Urinary infection.
